claims.text: Rapid carbothermal shock treatment of precursor NM-HEAs produces three-dimensional nanoporous frameworks.
The resulting nanoporous frameworks enhance catalytic performance.
Increased porosity and exposure of active sites are responsible for the enhanced catalytic performance.
The precursor contains both noble and sacrificial metal elements before phase stabilization.
Carbothermal shock treatment involves ultrafast heating followed by immediate quenching.
High-temperature shock induces severe lattice distortion in the NM-HEA precursor.
High-temperature shock triggers in situ dealloying.
Selective dealloying forms a three-dimensional nanoporous framework.
A distorted lattice structure is stabilized during formation of the nanoporous framework.
Rapid heating and quenching promote selective removal of sacrificial metals through in situ dealloying.
The porous structure provides a higher density of accessible catalytic sites.
Shock-treated NM-HEAs have significantly greater catalytic activity than counterparts prepared by conventional annealing and chemical dealloying.
Traditional slow annealing followed by selective chemical etching yields less porous structures and lower surface area.
Formation of the desired nanoporous framework requires an alloy containing both noble and sacrificial elements.
Temperature, duration, and cooling rate must exceed unspecified thresholds to induce the required lattice distortion.
Shock treatment outside the required parameter ranges may produce incomplete framework formation or phase segregation.
The optimal shock temperature, duration, and cooling rate remain to be established.
The influence of alloy composition on framework formation remains to be rigorously established.
